title: API Versioning & Evolution
summary: Changing an API without breaking the clients that are still on the old contract — versioning strategies, the backward-compatible-vs-breaking line, and how to sunset an old version.

slides.markdown:
Once an API has real clients, you can't just change it — a mobile app on last year's version, a partner's integration, and this morning's web release might all be hitting the same endpoint at once. **Versioning** is how you change the contract without breaking whoever hasn't moved yet.

Think of it like changing a public road's rules: you can't retroactively make every driver already on the highway obey a new sign — you post the new rule, give people time to adapt, and only remove the old lane once traffic has actually moved.

slides.sectionTitle: Why APIs must change without breaking existing clients
slides.markdown:
Unlike your own frontend, you usually can't force every consumer of an API to upgrade the moment you ship a change. Mobile apps sit on old versions until users update (which some never do); third-party integrations were built against today's contract and won't be rewritten on your schedule; even your own other services might deploy on a different cadence.

This means an API's contract is effectively a promise made to the past: anything a client could reasonably have relied on — a field's presence, its type, a status code's meaning — has to keep working, or you've broken someone silently, often without any error visible to you until support tickets show up.

Versioning exists to let you keep that promise for existing clients while still letting the API evolve for new ones.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: URI versioning vs header versioning vs no versioning
slides.markdown:
| | URI versioning | Header versioning | No versioning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Example | `/v2/orders` | `Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2` | `/orders`, changes made backward-compatible only |
| Visibility | Obvious in logs, bookmarks, docs | Invisible unless you inspect headers | N/A — one contract, forever additive |
| Caching | Each version is a distinct cacheable URL | Same URL, cache keys must include the header | Simplest — one URL, one cache entry |
| Client burden | Must edit the URL to move versions | Must set a header correctly | None — but the API can only ever add, never change |

**How to decide:** URI versioning is the pragmatic default — it's visible, simple to route, and simple to reason about in logs. Header versioning appeals to purists (the resource's identity shouldn't change with its representation) but is easy to get wrong silently. "No versioning" is viable only if you have strict discipline about never making a breaking change, ever.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: two client versions hitting compatible API versions
slides.markdown:
![v1 and v2 app versions both succeeding against the same backend](assets/concurrent-versions.svg)

An old app version, still installed on some users' phones, keeps calling `/v1/orders` and gets the response shape it was built against. A newer app version calls `/v2/orders` and gets the new shape. Both run against the same backend infrastructure at the same time — nobody is forced to upgrade before their next request works.

The backend team's job is maintaining both contracts concurrently until `/v1/orders`'s traffic is low enough to retire.

slides.sectionTitle: Backward-compatible changes vs breaking changes: the rule of thumb
slides.markdown:
A change is **backward-compatible** if every existing client keeps working, unmodified, after it ships. Adding a new optional field, adding a new endpoint, or adding a new enum value a client doesn't yet expect (as long as the client tolerates unknown values) are all typically safe.

A change is **breaking** if any client that follows the documented contract could stop working. Removing a field, renaming a field, changing a field's type (string to int), tightening a previously-optional field to required, or changing a status code's meaning are all breaking — even if it feels like a "small" fix.

The rule of thumb: if you can describe the change as "we only added something," it's probably safe; if the description is "we changed or removed something a client might read," assume it's breaking until proven otherwise.

slides.sectionTitle: Deprecation strategy: sunset headers, timelines, communicating change
slides.markdown:
Retiring an old API version is its own project, not a flag flip. Standard practice: announce the deprecation with a concrete date, add a `Sunset` (or `Deprecation`) response header to every call on the old version so automated tooling — not just a changelog nobody reads — can detect it, and email or notify known integrators directly.

Before the actual cutoff, monitor real traffic on the old version — if a major partner is still sending thousands of requests a day a week before sunset, that's a signal to either extend the timeline or escalate directly, not silently break them on the deadline.

The timeline itself should be generous enough for the slowest realistic consumer to react — weeks for an internal service, often months for a public API with third-party integrators who need their own release cycle to adapt.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a "breaking" field change shipped as a non-breaking patch
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We just changed `total` from a string `\"19.99\"` to a number `19.99` — that's basically the same value, it's fine to ship without a version bump."

**Why it's wrong:** a client's code that calls `.split()` or expects a JSON string type will throw or silently misbehave the instant the field's type changes, regardless of how "equivalent" the value looks to a human. Type changes are breaking changes by definition, even when the underlying meaning hasn't moved.

**Correct model:** any change to a field's presence, name, or type is breaking, full stop — the fix is to add a *new* field (`total_amount` as a number) alongside the old one, deprecate the old one on its own timeline, and let clients migrate at their own pace instead of finding out at 2am.
